prospect.name: Siddiq Farid
prospect.occupation: Self-employed business owner — spent seven years working for himself building a business, works remotely with about 80 percent of his work done on a phone or tablet, and travels for work. Previously lived in Doha 2016-17.
prospect.family_status: Married, four children — 16, 13, 22 months and a two-week-old newborn. In-laws currently staying to help. The 13-year-old plays junior-level professional cricket and is touring London in two weeks.
prospect.training_background: Two years of consistent, self-directed change. Peaked around 100 kg, dropped to 80 kg and has held it for about a year; original target was 70 kg but the focus shifted to body composition four to five months ago. Gym three to four times a week — upper, lower and full body days, 20 to 30 minutes of weights plus 30 to 60 minutes of incline walking — and 10,000 steps most days. Started kettlebells about a month before the call using two he already owned, running a self-designed eight-exercise circuit (swing, clean, shoulder press, row, deadlift, helicopter, pullover, plank row, push-up, two-minute farmer's walk) at 16-20 kg, two to three rounds. Can now do 10 chin-ups. Former squash and badminton player; plays recreational tennis with his son twice a week and golf.
prospect.medical: Right shoulder impingement — "there's an impingement over here, lacking space" — caused about a month before the call by taking up tennis. It became severe: "there was a period where I was in excruciating pain... I couldn't do anything, I couldn't sleep." Physiotherapy did not help. A doctor administered a steroid injection to reduce inflammation, against his own stated preference: "even the doctor was like, listen, I'm not in favour of this. But I need to give you something to make sure that at least it responds." The doctor also flagged a contingency — "if the steroid doesn't work, that means there's some bigger problem we need to go fix properly." The prospect reports it has been fine since but notes "that's one thing that could potentially come back." Two prior surgeries on the left ankle for stretched ligaments, the last in 2016, asymptomatic since, but he has stopped running and hardcore sport as a result. Chronic stiffness in shoulders, core, lower back and hips from desk and phone work. Sleep badly disrupted for the last two weeks by the newborn — "my sleep has been horrible."

signals: Already succeeded on his own and is now seeking marginal gain: down 20 kg over two years, held for a year, and explicitly reframing away from weight — "it's more so, oh, not the weight, but it's the body composition."
Price read as a quality and logistics question rather than a barrier: "I'm not too concerned about the amount, I'll be very honest" and "It's a timing thing more than the affordability thing."
Frames the purchase as capability acquisition, not rescue: "it's another arsenal in my tool belt... I'm equipping myself with another tool that's going to stay with me for the rest of my life."
Uses a consultant mental model for buying expertise, which the rep matched — he is a business owner who understands paying to shortcut a learning curve.

Carries a rebuilder history (100 kg, camera-shy, clothes kept in the closet that no longer fit) but has already done the rebuilding himself, so the current posture is optimizer rather than the_rebuilder.

objections.raw_quote: let me just confirm with the missus, and then I'll drop off. What's the next step? What's the process?
objections.rep_response: Ran a good portion of the play. Confirmed the prospect's own belief first — "I understand that you're positive about it, that you can get to your goals with Trevor" — asked whether he had already discussed it with her, and asked "when you talk to her today, like, do you feel that there might be any potential obstacles?" He then pre-framed how the request would land without context: "the missus, what hears is, okay, so my husband wants to get a fitness program for 6K... what's usually the answer. Like, are you crazy?" When the prospect raised that his wife had just given birth and needs to get in shape herself, the rep amplified rather than resolved it: "She might be opposed to that, actually." No deposit-with-refund fallback and no ownership reframe were offered.

It would be like $1,200 per month" — which over six months totals $7,200, or $1,200 above list. And the option the rep recommended: "the best option that I would suggest is just split it in half. So you pay $3,000 now and $3,000 in 30 days, and there's no interest on that." The rep also asked whether the prospect had used third-party financing partners; he declined. No figures were quoted for the financing option on this call.

Counter-evidence: he leaves with a materially wrong number in his head. The monthly plan was quoted at $1,200 and he twice restated it as $1,000 without correction, so the figure he is taking to his wife is $200 a month below the one quoted.

Counter-evidence: two live competing claims on the same money — a son's cricket tour to London in two weeks and his wife's own post-partum wish to get back in shape, which he raised himself as a likely objection from her.

notable.note: Two things a principal should see. First, the monthly payment option was quoted at $1,200 per month — $7,200 over six months against a $6,000 list price — and the prospect then twice described it back as $1,000 a month, uncorrected, immediately before going away to present the number to his wife. Second, this prospect had a steroid injection into a right shoulder impingement roughly a month before the call, after physiotherapy failed and after a period of excruciating pain, with his own doctor flagging that failure of the injection would mean "some bigger problem we need to go fix properly". He is currently pressing 20 kg overhead. The rep noticed the loads — "the weights that you said, they seem pretty high already" — and responded by promising Trevor would check his form. No clinical clearance was sought or mentioned. On process this is otherwise one of the better calls in the batch: the reflect-back at 00:22:13 was genuinely good, the OD busy-season move ran and landed, and the accountability pillar was the reason the prospect said he reached out.

quality.notes: Continuous inversion, resolved from content throughout. Notable examples: "I'm a very tall guy. I'm a short guy. I'm like 5'5"" at 00:01:04 is a single speaker self-correcting or an ASR artefact, read as height 5'5"; "My target weight when I started, was like 70" at 00:03:25 sits under the rep's label but is the prospect; "So the best option that I would suggest is just split it in half" at 00:50:08 is labelled as the prospect but is plainly the rep. The pricing exchange from 00:49:00 to 00:50:36 is the worst-affected passage — an unpunctuated run-on merging both speakers, from which the $1,200 per month figure and the $3,000 plus $3,000 split were resolved by content; both attributions are unambiguous on sense but the passage is not clean. The rep also appears to address the prospect as "Ben" at 00:00:48, almost certainly an ASR rendering of "then". Other corruptions include "missiles" and "nurses" for missus, "aggregated" for aggravated, and "body fight" for body fat. No evidence of dropped audio or truncation.
